Curtain Bangs by Face Shape

A parted fringe that starts shorter near the center and lengthens toward the sides.

Curtain bangs are a fringe choice, not a complete haircut. The shortest piece, width of the central opening and length of the sides all change the result. Compare those three decisions before choosing a reference photo.

Curtain Bangs variations for seven face shapes

Use these suggestions to choose where the haircut adds width or leaves the outline visible. You can prefer a different effect.

Oval face

Choose the shortest point for your forehead height and routine; a light, cheekbone-length version is a less dramatic starting point.

Round face

Keep a visible central opening and longer side pieces. Avoid a dense curtain that spreads horizontally at the cheeks if width is not your goal.

Square face

Use soft, separated edges and a curve past the cheekbones rather than a blunt fringe line.

Oblong face

A slightly shorter, fuller curtain can cover more of the forehead; avoid pairing it with a very tall crown.

Heart face

Keep the center light and let the longer sides skim the temples; ask for an opening that follows your natural part.

Diamond face

Keep some softness beside the temples and let the longest pieces continue below the cheekbones.

Triangle face

A fuller upper fringe can add forehead width; keep the side pieces from forming a heavy block at the jaw.

Set the shortest piece first

Ask where the shortest piece will sit with your hair dry and in its natural part. A shorter fringe covers more forehead; a longer one leaves more of it visible and may be easier to tuck aside. Begin longer if you want room to adjust the cut after seeing how it behaves.

The longer sides should connect to the haircut you already wear. A disconnected fringe can need a different styling routine from the rest of your hair. Bring a photograph of your normal hairstyle, including how you tie it back.

Check your part and growth pattern

A reference image may have an open center even if your hair naturally parts to one side. Ask your stylist to test the section without forcing it into position. The fringe can be slightly off-center; it does not have to form two identical halves.

Cowlicks and curls affect how the shortest pieces lift. For a curly fringe, assess the dry curl and expected shrinkage before removing length. Coily fringes may need a specialist dry-cut consultation; this starter finder does not yet model those variations.

Plan for the fringe between washes

The front of the hair can need a reset before the rest does. Decide whether a quick wetting and air-dry fits your routine or whether you are comfortable using a dryer and brush. Do not choose a heat-styled reference and expect exactly the same shape without styling.

A longer curtain usually blends into the sides as it grows, but maintaining a specific short opening still means trimming the fringe. Ask about the salon's fringe-trim routine before you commit.

Questions about curtain bangs

Do curtain bangs only suit oval faces?

No. Adjusting the opening, shortest point and side length creates different versions. Face shape is a starting point for those choices, not an eligibility rule.

Are curtain bangs low maintenance?

They can grow out gradually, but the daily routine depends on your part, texture and desired finish. A polished sweep may need a reset even when the rest of the hair does not.

Can I keep my current haircut?

Often, yes. Ask how the longer sides of the fringe will connect to your existing length and whether they will still tuck back or fit in a ponytail.

How these suggestions were written

We match the seven broad contour profiles to adjustable haircut features. The rule weights are authored suggestions; they have not been fitted to client outcomes. Your stylist can account for hair density, growth patterns and the finish you want.

Allure: curtain-bang definitions and stylist advice: Reference for the graduated fringe and the role of texture and growth patterns. Our match labels and seven-shape variations are editorial rules.

Before your appointment

  • Bring a photo of your usual, unstyled hair.
  • Choose the length you need for tying or tucking back.
  • Ask to see how the ends sit when dry.
  • Discuss styling time and regular trims.

Maintenance: medium. A fringe often needs a daily reset and more frequent trims than the rest of the cut. On curls, choose the length while dry.
